title: String Compression
statement:
Run-length encode the character array `chars` in place. Split `chars` into maximal runs of equal neighbouring characters and, going from left to right, emit for each run:

- the run's character, and
- if the run is longer than 1, its length in decimal, one digit per array slot (a run of 12 emits `"1"` and `"2"`).

Store the emitted characters at the front of `chars` and return their count `k`. Only `chars[0..k-1]` is checked; whatever is left after it does not matter. Solve it with only O(1) extra memory beyond `chars` itself.
constraints: chars[i] is a lowercase or uppercase English letter, a digit, or a symbol
notes:
## Intuition

The easy way is to build the compressed string in a separate buffer and copy it back, but that uses O(n) extra memory. It is not needed: a run of length `c` turns into at most `c` characters (one character, plus `String(c).length` digits only when `c >= 2`), so the compressed text never gets ahead of the part of the array still to be read. Two pointers moving in the same direction can therefore overwrite `chars` from the front as they go.

## Approach

1. `read` scans the input and `write` marks where the next output character goes; both start at 0.
2. At each new run, remember its character in `current` and advance `read` while it still sees `current`, counting the run's length in `count`.
3. Write `current` at `write` and move `write` on.
4. If `count > 1`, write each digit of `String(count)` the same way.
5. When `read` reaches the end, `write` is the compressed length; return it.

## Example 1, step by step

`chars = ["a","a","b","b","c","c","c"]`.

- `read = 0`: `current = "a"`, `count = 2`, `read = 2`. Write `"a"`, `"2"` at 0 and 1; `write = 2`.
- `read = 2`: `current = "b"`, `count = 2`, `read = 4`. Write `"b"`, `"2"` at 2 and 3; `write = 4`.
- `read = 4`: `current = "c"`, `count = 3`, `read = 7`. Write `"c"`, `"3"` at 4 and 5; `write = 6`.

`read` hit the end, so the answer is 6 with `["a","2","b","2","c","3"]` at the front.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): `read` passes over every character once and `write` never moves more than `read`.
- Space: O(1): only a few counters (the digits of `count` are at most 4 characters).

## Pitfalls

- A run of length 1 gets no digit; `"a1"` is wrong.
- Counts of 10 or more take several slots: write every digit, not `count` as one element.
- The same character can appear in separate runs (`"aabaa"`); only neighbouring equal characters merge.
- Digits can also be input characters, so do not try to tell counts and characters apart by looking at them.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `read` | next input position to scan |
| `write` | next output position, and finally the compressed length |
| `current` | the character of the run being read |
| `count` | the length of that run |
| `digit` | one decimal digit of `count` being written |

narration.2: write is where the next compressed character goes.
narration.3: read is the next input character to look at; it always stays at or ahead of write.
narration.5: Each pass of this loop handles one whole run of equal characters.
narration.6: Remember the character this run is made of.
narration.8: Keep reading while the next character still belongs to the run.
narration.9: Step past one character of the run...
narration.12: Every run puts its character into the output first.
narration.14: A run of one character gets no count after it.
narration.15: Write the run length one decimal digit at a time, so 12 becomes '1' then '2'.
narration.16: Place this digit at the write position; read is already past it, so nothing unread is lost.
narration.21: write now equals the length of the compressed prefix.
